newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea's pampered ship workers shun strikes.
newsitem.headline: South Korea's pampered ship workers shun strikes.

text.p: Kim Hung-sik has never risen past the rank of driver in his long career with Hyundai Heavy Industries, but he has been richly rewarded -- a roomy apartment, his own car and almost eight weeks of annual leave.

One of his daughters is studying at Ulsan University, owned by the giant Hyundai Group. His home and car are heavily-subsidised by the company. College education is free, as is medical care in company-run hospitals.
"I like it here," he said, gesturing over the balcony of his Hyundai-built apartment towards green hills. "It's very convenient for the health club."
Workers like Kim explain why the latest outburst of industrial unrest in South Korea is sputtering out after four inconclusive weeks of confrontation between labour unions and the government.
Employees at Hyundai Heavy, the world's biggest shipbuilder, were so keen to remain on the job they drove a bulldozer through barricades put up by a handful of strikers at the gate.
Kim had few qualms about breaking the strike called by the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions that has a grip on all Hyundai plants: he quit the union three years ago.
"I felt I was part of management," he explained. "I didn't feel I belonged in the union."
A controversial labour bill that sparked the strikes has been sent back to parliament by President Kim Young-sam, who has conceded it should be revised but has refused union demands to scrap it.
Kim's ruling camp is now groping towards compromise with opposition parties over the law.
The bill sought to make it easier for companies to lay off workers, adopt flexible work hours and hire temporary staff.

Yet none of these provisions has caused much concern in Ulsan, where Hyundai also operates the nation's number one car plant. Hyundai already employs transient labour on production lines, and it has subtle ways of getting rid of staff it no longer needs, according to union leaders.
Anger is focused more on clauses of the bill that threaten union power by allowing companies to replace strikers and making it illegal for firms to pay full-time union organisers.

Public sympathy was with Ulsan workers back in 1987 when they rose up against military-style work discipline and low pay, using flaming oil drums and giant metal cutters as weapons against riot police sent in to crush them.
Now the once down-trodden shipyard and car workers are fighting a more lonely battle. There is growing resentment at their high pay, and generous perks and privileges.

Foreman Choi Mu-ryung, for instance, reckoned that when his basic salary, bonuses and various subsidisies were all added up, his monthly package from Hyundai Heavy was worth 4.2 million won ($5,000). Per capita income in South Korea is $10,000.
"I've come a long way," said Choi.
Perhaps too far. Even as Hyundai Heavy struggles to stay afloat in an industry battered by falling prices for new ships, it continues to pamper its workers with new luxuries.

Having built 16,000 apartments and four "welfare centres" complete with 10-pin bowling alleys, skating rinks, cinemas and American-style steak houses, construction has begun on a fifth centre, this one boasting indoor soccer pitches.
For Hyundai spouses, the centres offer courses in flower arranging and cooking.

And within sight of giant cranes swinging over dry docks where their husbands weld together supertankers, the wives spend their days on outdoor tennis courts, working with coaches to improve their game.

"We've learnt many lessons from past strike experiences," said Lee Gyun-jae, who is in charge of "corporate culture" at Hyundai Heavy. "We have 27,000 workers, and only about 100 joined the latest strikes".
